mainTopic: How the מגילה must be read and written: order and pauses, a flawed or unfinished מגילה, writing from memory, and invalid writing materials
overview: The amud opens with the end of a ברייתא: reading the מגילה out of order (סירוסין) does not count. רבי מונא adds that even with breaks (סירוגין), a pause as long as it takes to read the whole מגילה forces the reader to start over. רב יוסף rules like him and tells אביי that the pause is measured by the whole מגילה. The גמרא then brings conflicting versions of how רב and שמואל ruled. רב יוסף accepts רב ביבי's version because שמואל tends to follow a lone, stricter opinion, and he proves this from a משנה in יבמות. Next come ברייתות about a מגילה with missing letters or verses, and about a reader who skips a verse or arrives in the middle. The גמרא defines the משנה's מתנמנם and explains how someone writing a מגילה can fulfill the מצוה: he reads from a complete מגילה in front of him. This leads to רבי יוחנן's rule against writing even one letter from memory, the stories of רבי מאיר and רב חננאל, and the exception for תפילין and מזוזות. The amud ends by defining the invalid writing materials listed in the משנה.

steps.title: Reading the מגילה out of order does not count
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא finishes its rule: if one reads the מגילה out of order (סירוסין), he has not fulfilled his obligation.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he read it out of order, he has not fulfilled his obligation.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the end of a ברייתא that began just before our passage. It said that reading with breaks (סירוגין) counts, but reading out of order (סירוסין) does not count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מגילה must be read in its written order, so mixing up the words or verses ruins the reading completely. Taking breaks does not change the order, which is why the first half of the ברייתא allowed it. The next step limits even that allowance.

keyTerms.meaning: Out of order, with words or verses switched around
With breaks or pauses in between parts of the reading
He has not fulfilled his obligation

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up סירוסין and סירוגין. סירוסין means out of order, and that is invalid. סירוגין means with pauses, and that is basically valid.

phrases.english: Out of order, he has not fulfilled his obligation.
phrases.notes: The words on the previous amud were: קראה סירוגין יצא (if he read it with breaks, he has fulfilled it).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא's contrast between סירוגין and סירוסין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Reading the מגילה out of order is invalid.

steps.title: A long enough pause means starting over
steps.stepSummary: רבי מונא, quoting רבי יהודה, says that even with breaks, if one pause lasted as long as it takes to read the whole מגילה, the reader must go back to the beginning.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מונא says in the name of רבי יהודה: Even with breaks, if he paused long enough to finish the whole thing, he goes back to the beginning.
steps.whatsHappening: A second voice in the ברייתא adds a limit to the rule that reading with breaks is valid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion allowed breaks of any length. רבי מונא says that a pause long enough to read the entire מגילה cuts the reading apart, so the reading must be restarted. This makes רבי מונא a lone opinion that is stricter than the first one, and that point becomes important later in the sugya.

keyTerms.meaning: Long enough to finish all of it
He goes back to the beginning

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי מוּנָא אוֹמֵר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יְהוּדָה:
phrases.english: Rabbi Mona says in the name of Rabbi Yehuda:
Even with breaks,

phrases.aramaic: אִם שָׁהָה כְּדֵי לִגְמוֹר אֶת כּוּלָּהּ —
phrases.english: if he paused long enough to finish all of it,
he goes back to the beginning.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Puts a limit on the ברייתא's allowance for סירוגין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A pause as long as the time it takes to read the whole מגילה requires starting again from the beginning.
steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי מוּנָא אוֹמֵר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יְהוּדָה

steps.title: רב יוסף rules like רבי מונא
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף rules that the הלכה follows רבי מונא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: The law follows רבי מונא, who spoke in the name of רבי יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא gives a practical ruling on the ברייתא: the stricter view of רבי מונא is the הלכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a lone opinion does not win, but רב יוסף accepts the stricter limit. This sets up אביי's question about exactly how long the pause has to be.

keyTerms.meaning: The law follows the view of...

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:

phrases.aramaic: הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי מוּנָא שֶׁאָמַר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יְהוּדָה.
phrases.english: The law follows Rabbi Mona, who said it in the name of Rabbi Yehuda.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a practical ruling on רבי מונא's statement.
steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי מוּנָא

steps.title: How long is 'enough time to finish all of it'?
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks רב יוסף whether the length of the pause is measured from where the reader stopped until the end, or from the beginning of the מגילה until the end.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to רב יוסף: 'Long enough to finish all of it' means from where he is up to the end, or perhaps from the beginning to the end?
steps.whatsHappening: Now that the הלכה follows רבי מונא, אביי asks a clarifying question about how to measure the pause.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two possible measuring sticks. One is the time needed to read whatever is left, from where he stopped. The other is the time needed to read the entire מגילה. The question is about definition, not an attack on the ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: From the place where he is standing, meaning where he stopped

phrases.english: Abaye said to Rav Yosef:
'Long enough to finish all of it':
from where he is standing until the end,
or perhaps from the beginning to the end?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the precise meaning of the measurement in the ruling just given.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the length of the pause is measured by the rest of the מגילה or by the whole מגילה.

steps.title: Measured by the whole מגילה, so the rule stays fixed
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף answers that the pause is measured from beginning to end. Otherwise the length of the pause would change in every case.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: From the beginning to the end. Because if it were so (measured from where he stopped), you would be making your words into changing measurements.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף answers אביי: we use the time it takes to read the whole מגילה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If we measured from where he stopped, the allowed pause would be different every time, depending on how far along the reader was. חכמים prefer one fixed measurement that applies to everyone. So the standard is always the full reading time.

keyTerms.meaning: You have made your words depend on changing measurements

steps.whatToRemember: The length of pause that forces a restart is fixed: the time it takes to read the entire מגילה from beginning to end.

phrases.english: He said to him: From the beginning to the end,
because if so, you have given your words over to varying measures.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The time to read the whole מגילה, because a single fixed measurement is required.

steps.title: The סורא version: רב agrees with רבי מונא, שמואל disagrees
steps.stepSummary: Through a chain of tradition, רב rules like רבי מונא and שמואל rules against him. This is how they learned it in סורא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא said that רבי ירמיה בר אבא said that רב said: The law follows רבי מונא. And שמואל said: The law does not follow רבי מונא. This is how they taught it in סורא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a dispute between רב and שמואל about whether to follow רבי מונא, in the version taught in סורא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This adds the views of two major אמוראים on the same question. In this version רב is the stricter one and שמואל is the more lenient one. The phrase 'this is how they taught it in סורא' tells us that other versions are coming.

keyTerms.meaning: סורא, a major Babylonian yeshiva city

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rabbi Abba said that Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba said that Rav said:
The law follows Rabbi Mona.

phrases.aramaic: וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר: אֵין הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי מוּנָא.
phrases.english: And Shmuel said: The law does not follow Rabbi Mona.
In Sura they taught it this way.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings in the אמוראים' dispute about the same ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the סורא version, רב rules like רבי מונא and שמואל does not.
steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַב

steps.title: The פומבדיתא version: same positions, different chain of tradition
steps.stepSummary: In פומבדיתא the same positions were taught, but they were passed down through רב כהנא.
steps.simpleTranslation: In פומבדיתא they taught it like this: רב כהנא said that רב said: The law follows רבי מונא. And שמואל said: The law does not follow רבי מונא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the version taught in פומבדיתא. The positions are the same as in סורא, and only the person who passed it down is different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The only change is who transmitted רב's view: רב כהנא instead of the chain through רבי ירמיה בר אבא. So two yeshivos agree that רב is strict and שמואל is lenient. This sets up the opposite version that comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: פומבדיתא, the other major Babylonian yeshiva city

phrases.english: In Pumbedita they taught it this way:
Rav Kahana said that Rav said:
The law follows Rabbi Mona.

phrases.aramaic: וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר: אֵין הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי מוּנָא.
phrases.english: And Shmuel said: The law does not follow Rabbi Mona.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second version that keeps the same positions but has a different chain of tradition.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the פומבדיתא version, through רב כהנא, רב rules like רבי מונא and שמואל does not.

steps.title: רב ביבי teaches the positions reversed
steps.stepSummary: רב ביבי's version switches the positions: רב does not follow רבי מונא, and שמואל does.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ביבי taught it the opposite way: רב said: The law does not follow רבי מונא. And שמואל said: The law follows רבי מונא.
steps.whatsHappening: A third version flips who holds what. This sets up רב יוסף's decision about which version is correct.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now there is a real contradiction about which of the two אמוראים was the strict one. Here שמואל is the one who follows the stricter lone opinion. We need a way to decide between the versions.

phrases.english: Rav Beivai taught it the opposite way:

phrases.aramaic: רַב אָמַר: אֵין הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי מוּנָא,
phrases.english: Rav said: The law does not follow Rabbi Mona,
and Shmuel said: The law follows Rabbi Mona.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contradicts the two earlier versions by reversing the positions.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In רב ביבי's version, רב rejects רבי מונא and שמואל accepts him.

steps.title: Follow רב ביבי's version, because שמואל takes lone opinions seriously
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף decides that רב ביבי's version is correct. We know שמואל tends to take into account a lone, stricter opinion.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: Hold on to רב ביבי's version, because it is שמואל who takes an individual opinion into account.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף chooses among the three versions and gives his reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מונא is a single opinion that is stricter than the first opinion in the ברייתא. Since שמואל is known to worry about such lone strict views, it fits him to rule like רבי מונא, which is exactly what רב ביבי's version says. The גמרא will now prove this habit of שמואל's.

keyTerms.meaning: Hold it in your hand, meaning accept it as correct
Takes into account, is concerned for

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a method the גמרא uses: when versions of a tradition conflict, it picks the one that fits what we already know about how a particular חכם tends to rule.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
Hold Rav Beivai's version in your hand,
for it is Shmuel who takes an individual opinion into account.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides between the conflicting versions.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רב ביבי's version is accepted: שמואל rules like רבי מונא.

steps.title: Proof from the case of a שומרת יבם
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא cites a משנה in יבמות. There, following the lone opinion of רבי יהודה בן בתירה, a brother who married the sister of a שומרת יבם is told to wait. This begins the proof that שמואל takes lone opinions into account.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned in a משנה: A woman waiting for her brother-in-law, whose brother-in-law's brother betrothed her sister. In the name of רבי יהודה בן בתירה they said: We tell him, 'Wait until your older brother acts.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts bringing a source to prove that שמואל pays attention to lone opinions. The proof continues next, where שמואל will rule like this lone opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A widow waiting for יבום is connected in some way to all the brothers. That is why רבי יהודה בן בתירה says another brother should not yet marry her sister. רבי יהודה בן בתירה is a lone opinion against the חכמים, who say only the oldest brother is connected to her. The proof will show that שמואל follows him.

keyTerms.meaning: A widow waiting for her late husband's brother to do יבום or חליצה
An act, here meaning יבום or חליצה

steps.confusionAlert: This topic from יבמות has nothing to do with the מגילה. It is brought only to show how שמואל treats a lone opinion in general.

phrases.english: As we learned in a Mishnah:

phrases.aramaic: שׁוֹמֶרֶת יָבָם שֶׁקִּידֵּשׁ אָחִיו אֶת אֲחוֹתָהּ,
phrases.english: A woman waiting for her brother-in-law, whose brother-in-law's brother betrothed her sister:

phrases.aramaic: מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתִירָה אָמְרוּ,
phrases.english: In the name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira they said:
We say to him:

phrases.aramaic: הַמְתֵּן עַד שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה אָחִיךָ הַגָּדוֹל מַעֲשֶׂה.
phrases.english: Wait until your older brother acts.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts supporting the claim about שמואל made in the previous step.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that שמואל takes a lone opinion into account.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in יבמות (41a) with the lone opinion of רבי יהודה בן בתירה. שמואל's ruling on it appears next.
steps.triggerLanguage: דִּתְנַן: שׁוֹמֶרֶת יָבָם שֶׁקִּידֵּשׁ אָחִיו אֶת אֲחוֹתָהּ

steps.title: שמואל rules like the lone stricter opinion
steps.stepSummary: שמואל rules like רבי יהודה בן בתירה, who stands alone. This completes the proof that שמואל takes a lone, stricter opinion into account.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: The הלכה follows רבי יהודה בן בתירה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the proof it started in Step 10. שמואל rules like the single stricter opinion of רבי יהודה בן בתירה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, רבי יהודה בן בתירה stood alone with a stricter ruling about the brother of a שומרת יבם. שמואל rules like him anyway. This shows שמואל is willing to follow a lone stricter opinion, which fits רב ביבי's version, where שמואל follows the lone opinion of רבי מונא.

keyTerms.meaning: A single חכם who stands against the majority

steps.whatToRemember: שמואל takes a lone, stricter opinion seriously. That is why רב יוסף accepted רב ביבי's version, in which שמואל follows רבי מונא.

phrases.english: Shmuel said:
The halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira.
phrases.notes: This is the lone, stricter opinion, and ruling like it is what finishes the proof.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתִירָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the proof begun with the משנה in Step 10
steps.raayaObject: The claim that שמואל takes a lone stricter opinion into account, supporting רב ביבי's version
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמואל's ruling like רבי יהודה בן בתירה on the משנה in יבמות

steps.title: A מגילה missing letters or verses is still valid
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that if the scribe left out letters or verses and the reader said them by heart, the reader has fulfilled the מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: If the scribe left out letters or verses from the מגילה, and the reader said them by heart the way a translator speaks, he has fulfilled his obligation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new topic. It quotes a ברייתא that says small gaps in a written מגילה do not ruin the reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A מתורגמן said his translation from memory, not from a written text. Here the reader does the same for the missing words, and the reading still counts. So a few missing letters or verses do not make the מגילה invalid.

keyTerms.meaning: The scribe who wrote the מגילה
A translator who said the Aramaic translation aloud from memory

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
If the scribe left out from it (the Megilla)
letters or verses
and the reader read them
like a translator who translates (from memory),
he has fulfilled his obligation.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הִשְׁמִיט בָּהּ סוֹפֵר אוֹתִיּוֹת אוֹ פְּסוּקִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about a flawed מגילה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Missing letters or verses, recited by heart, do not invalidate the reading of the מגילה.

steps.title: Challenge: unclear letters make a מגילה invalid
steps.stepSummary: A different ברייתא says that if letters are blurred or torn and cannot be made out, the מגילה is invalid. This seems to clash with the first ברייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: If the מגילה had letters that were blurred or torn, then if their outline can still be seen it is valid, and if not, it is invalid!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the first ברייתא with another ברייתא that seems to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Blurred letters that cannot be seen are basically missing letters. If missing letters make the מגילה invalid here, how could the first ברייתא say even whole missing verses are fine? The two sources seem to contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: Their outline can still be seen

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
If there were letters in it
that were blurred or torn,
if their outline is visible, it is valid,
and if not, it is invalid!
phrases.notes: Unreadable letters count as missing, so missing letters seem to invalidate the מגילה.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי: הָיוּ בָּהּ אוֹתִיּוֹת מְטוּשְׁטָשׁוֹת אוֹ מְקוֹרָעוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ברייתא in Step 12
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that a מגילה missing letters or verses is still valid
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another ברייתא invalidates a מגילה whose letters cannot be seen, which is the same as missing letters.

steps.title: Answer: a whole damaged מגילה versus a small part
steps.stepSummary: The two ברייתות speak about different cases. Damage throughout the whole מגילה makes it invalid. A gap in only part of it is fine.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult: This ברייתא (invalid) is when the damage is throughout all of it. That ברייתא (valid) is when only part of it is missing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction by saying each ברייתא is talking about a different situation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If letters are unreadable throughout the whole מגילה, there is not really a written מגילה at all, so it is invalid. If only some letters or verses are missing, the מגילה is still basically complete, and the reader can say the gaps by heart.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult (introduces an answer)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up which ברייתא is which. 'All of it' explains the ברייתא that says invalid (Step 13). 'Part of it' explains the ברייתא that says valid (Step 12).

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this one is about all of it,
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא that says it's invalid: the damage runs through the whole מגילה.

phrases.english: and that one is about part of it.
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא that says it's valid: only part of it is missing.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא בְּכוּלַּהּ, הָא בְּמִקְצָתַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 13
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each source refers to a different amount of damage
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות disagree about whether missing letters invalidate a מגילה.
steps.terutzMaskana: Damage throughout the whole מגילה invalidates it. Missing material in only part of it does not.
steps.whatToRemember: A small gap in a מגילה is fine if the reader says it by heart. Damage throughout the whole מגילה makes it invalid.

steps.title: A reader who skipped a verse must go back and continue from there
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that a reader who skipped a verse may not finish and then go back to read only that verse. He must return to that verse and read on from there.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: If the reader skipped one verse, he should not say, 'I will read all of it and afterward read that verse.' Rather, he reads from that verse onward.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about the order of reading the מגילה. It teaches what to do if the reader skips a verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מגילה must be read in its proper order. Reading the skipped verse at the end would put it out of order. So the reader goes back to the skipped verse and reads everything after it again.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
If the reader skipped one verse in it,
he should not say: I will read all of it
and afterward I will read that verse,
rather, he reads from that verse onward.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הִשְׁמִיט בָּהּ הַקּוֹרֵא פָּסוּק אֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New ברייתא on a related topic. The mistake here is by the reader, not the scribe.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The מגילה must be read in order. A skipped verse is fixed by going back to it and reading onward from there.
steps.whyThisMatters: This applies the rule from Step 1, that reading the מגילה out of order (סירוסין) does not count, to the practical case of a skipped verse.

steps.title: Arriving halfway: start from the beginning
steps.stepSummary: Someone who comes in after the congregation has read half may not read the second half with them and then make up the first half. He must read the whole מגילה in order from the start.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he entered the synagogue and found that the congregation had read half of it, he should not say, 'I will read the second half with the congregation and afterward read the first half.' Rather, he reads it from its beginning to its end.
steps.whatsHappening: The same ברייתא gives a second case that applies the same rule about order.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Reading the second half first and the first half afterward is reading out of order. So the latecomer must read the whole מגילה from start to finish in the right sequence.

keyTerms.meaning: From its beginning until its end

steps.whatToRemember: The מגילה must be read in its proper order. You cannot read later parts first and fill in earlier parts afterward.

phrases.english: If he entered the synagogue
and found a congregation that had read half of it,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יֹאמַר: אֶקְרָא חֶצְיָהּ עִם הַצִּבּוּר
phrases.english: he should not say: I will read half with the congregation
and afterward I will read the other half,
rather, he reads it
from its beginning until its end.

steps.triggerLanguage: נִכְנַס לְבֵית הַכְּנֶסֶת וּמָצָא צִבּוּר שֶׁקָּרְאוּ חֶצְיָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second case in the same ברייתא, applying the same rule about order
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A latecomer must read the entire מגילה in order from the beginning. He may not read the halves out of sequence.

steps.title: What counts as dozing off?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case of reading while dozing and asks what that state actually looks like.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: one who reads while dozing off has fulfilled the מצוה. What exactly is 'dozing off'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a line from the משנה and asks for a definition of מתנמנם. This sets up רב אשי's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being sound asleep is clearly not enough, and being fully awake is clearly fine. The גמרא wants to know the exact in-between state the משנה approved.

keyTerms.meaning: what are the circumstances? (asking for a definition)

phrases.english: One who is dozing has fulfilled, etc.
What are the circumstances of 'dozing'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to a new clause of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A definition of the state called מתנמנם.

steps.title: רב אשי defines dozing
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי: half-asleep and half-awake. He answers when called and remembers when reminded, but cannot give a reasoned answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: He is asleep but not fully asleep, and awake but not fully awake. When people call him, he answers. He cannot give a reasoned reply, but when people remind him of something, he remembers it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a clear description of the dozing state that the משנה approved.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The signs are practical. He responds to his name and recalls things when prompted, so he is not truly asleep. He just cannot think through an argument. That level of awareness is enough to count as reading the מגילה.

keyTerms.meaning: to give back a reasoned answer

steps.whatToRemember: מתנמנם means he responds when called and remembers when reminded, but cannot reason. Someone in that state who reads the מגילה has fulfilled the מצוה.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
Asleep yet not asleep,
awake yet not awake,
that when they call him, he answers,
but he does not know how to give a reasoned reply,
and when they remind him, he remembers.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: נִים וְלָא נִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Half-asleep and half-awake. He responds and recalls when reminded, but cannot reason.

steps.title: How does a writer fulfill the מצוה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about someone writing, explaining or correcting a מגילה, and asks what the exact case is.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: if he was writing it, explaining it, or correcting it, and he had intent, he has fulfilled the מצוה. What is the case?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה and asks how this case works. This opens a discussion that tests possible answers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says intent is what makes the reading count. The גמרא wants to know what this writer was actually reading from, since that decides whether the reading can count at all.

keyTerms.meaning: he had intent (to fulfill the מצוה)

phrases.english: If he was writing it, explaining it, or correcting it,
if he had intent, he fulfilled, etc.
What are the circumstances?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next clause of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the writer was reading from when he read the words.

steps.title: Saying the verse first is reading by heart
steps.stepSummary: If he said each verse and then wrote it down, he was reciting from memory, so intent cannot help.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he said each verse out loud and then wrote it, what good is his intent? He said it by heart!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries one possible case and rejects it right away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he says the words before writing them, nothing is written yet, so he is saying them על פה. The מצוה requires reading from a written text, and intent cannot fix that. So this cannot be the משנה's case.

phrases.aramaic: אִי דְּקָא מְסַדַּר פְּסוּקָא פְּסוּקָא וְכָתֵב לַהּ,
phrases.english: If he says each verse and then writes it,
so what if he had intent?
It is by heart!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי דְּקָא מְסַדַּר פְּסוּקָא פְּסוּקָא וְכָתֵב לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests and rejects the first possible answer to step 19.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The case of saying each verse before writing it.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: That is reading by heart, which never fulfills the מצוה.

steps.title: Maybe he writes each verse, then reads it
steps.stepSummary: Second suggestion: he writes each verse first and then reads it from what he just wrote.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, he writes each verse and then reads it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a new case: he reads from the words he has just written. The next step will challenge this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Reversing the order fixes the 'by heart' problem, because now he reads from a written text. But that text is a מגילה still being written.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא דְּכָתֵב פְּסוּקָא פְּסוּקָא וְקָרֵי לֵיהּ,
phrases.english: Rather, he writes each verse and reads it,

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא דְּכָתֵב פְּסוּקָא פְּסוּקָא וְקָרֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the case rejected in step 20.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He writes a verse and then reads it from his own new writing.

steps.title: The מגילה must be fully written
steps.stepSummary: Challenge from רב: the מגילה must be written in full, even according to the view that one need only read from 'איש יהודי'.
steps.simpleTranslation: But does he really fulfill the מצוה? רבי חלבו said in the name of רב חמא בר גוריא, who said in the name of רב: The הלכה follows the view that one must read all of it. And even according to the view that one reads only from 'There was a certain Jew,' the מגילה must be written in full!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the case from step 21 using a ruling of רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 21's case, the מגילה is not finished while he reads from it. רב rules that the מגילה must be completely written for the reading to count, and this is true even by the lenient view about how much one must read. So reading from a half-written מגילה cannot fulfill the מצוה.

keyTerms.meaning: all of it, the whole מגילה
from 'There was a certain Jew' (אסתר ב:ה)

steps.confusionAlert: There are two separate questions here. One is how much you must READ (all of it, or from 'איש יהודי'). The other is how much must be WRITTEN. The scroll must be written in full by both views.

phrases.english: But does he fulfill his obligation?
But didn't Rabbi Ḥelbo say

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חָמָא בַּר גּוּרְיָא אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: that Rav Ḥama bar Gurya said that Rav said:
The halacha follows the one who says all of it.
And even according to the one who says 'from "a certain Jew"' —
it must be written in its entirety!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the case proposed in step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: The case where he writes each verse and reads from his new, unfinished מגילה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב requires a fully written מגילה, so reading from an unfinished one cannot fulfill the מצוה.

steps.title: He copies from a complete מגילה
steps.stepSummary: The case must be that a complete מגילה lies in front of him. He reads each verse from it and then copies it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, a complete מגילה lies in front of him. He reads each verse from it and then writes it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles on the case that avoids both problems.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He reads from a finished, written מגילה, so he is not reading by heart and not reading from an unfinished scroll. His copying is just what he does after each verse. With intent, his reading counts.
steps.whatToRemember: The writer in the משנה fulfills the מצוה only because he reads from a complete מגילה in front of him while copying it.

phrases.english: Rather: a Megillah is lying before him
and he reads from it verse by verse
and writes it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 22 with a new case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He reads from the new מגילה he is writing.
steps.terutzMaskana: He reads from a separate, complete מגילה in front of him and copies it.

steps.title: A proof for רבי יוחנן?
steps.stepSummary: Suggestion: the משנה supports רבי יוחנן's rule that one may not write even one letter without copying from a written text.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say this supports רבה בר בר חנה? For רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: It is forbidden to write even one letter not from a written text.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests that the case it just reached proves another אמורא's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's writer turned out to be copying from a written מגילה. That might show this is required, which is exactly רבי יוחנן's rule against writing from memory.

keyTerms.meaning: shall we say it supports him?

steps.whyThisMatters: רבי יוחנן's rule, that a scribe must copy from a written text, is a basic practice for writing sacred scrolls.

phrases.aramaic: לֵימָא מְסַיַּיע לֵיהּ לְרַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה,
phrases.english: Shall we say this supports Rabba bar bar Ḥana,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: for Rabba bar bar Ḥana said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
It is forbidden to write a single letter
not from a written text.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵימָא מְסַיַּיע לֵיהּ לְרַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the case reached in step 23 as possible support for another rule.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוחנן's ban on writing even one letter from memory.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's case, as explained in step 23: copying from a written מגילה.

steps.title: Maybe it just happened that way
steps.stepSummary: Rejection: perhaps the writer simply happened to be copying from a מגילה. That does not show it is required.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps it just happened to be so.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from step 24.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה needed a written מגילה in front of him only for the reading to count. It does not show that the writing itself had to be copied. Maybe in this case it simply happened that he was copying, so the משנה proves nothing about רבי יוחנן's rule.
steps.whatToRemember: The משנה does not prove רבי יוחנן's rule. The written מגילה was needed for the reading, and the copying may simply have happened that way.

phrases.english: Perhaps it just happened to him that way.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof offered in step 24.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof only. רבי יוחנן's rule itself is not rejected.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The case may describe what happened, not what is required.

steps.title: Returning to the rule: no writing even one letter from memory
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings back רבי יוחנן's rule so it can examine it on its own: one may not write even one letter of a holy text without copying it from a written text.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now to the matter itself. רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: It is forbidden to write even one letter unless you are copying from a written text.
steps.whatsHappening: The word גופא tells us the גמרא is now going back to a statement it mentioned earlier, so it can study that statement directly. This sets up the challenge that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the last step, this rule came up only as a possible proof from the משנה, and that proof was rejected. Now the rule itself is the topic. The rule is very strict: not even one letter may be written from memory.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The matter itself': a signal that the גמרא is returning to study a statement quoted earlier
Not from a written text, meaning written from memory

phrases.english: The matter itself:
Rabba bar bar Ḥana said
Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
It is forbidden to write a single letter
not from a written text.

steps.triggerLanguage: גּוּפָא, אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The rule was cited in step 24 as a possible proof. Now the גמרא returns to examine the rule itself.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: It is forbidden to write even one letter of a holy text without copying from a written text.

steps.title: Challenge from the story of רבי מאיר writing a מגילה from memory
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא tells that רבי מאיר wrote a מגילה from memory when none was available, and then read from it. This seems to contradict רבי יוחנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged this from a ברייתא. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר said: There was a story with רבי מאיר, who went to make the year a leap year in Asia. There was no מגילה there, so he wrote one from memory and read from it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן's rule with a story about רבי מאיר, who did exactly what the rule forbids.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן says not even one letter may be written from memory. Yet רבי מאיר wrote an entire מגילה from memory and used it for the מצוה of reading. If that was allowed, the rule looks wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: To make the year a leap year by adding a month
From his heart, meaning from memory

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar said:
There was an incident with Rabbi Meir
who went to make the year a leap year in Asia,
and there was no Megilla there,
so he wrote it from memory and read from it!
phrases.notes: Asia here probably means a place outside ארץ ישראל.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי, אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the rule stated in step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's rule that nothing may be written from memory
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי מאיר, a great תנא, wrote a whole מגילה from memory and read from it. That suggests writing from memory is allowed.

steps.title: רבי מאיר was different: his memory of the text was perfect
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו answers that רבי מאיר is an exception. The verse 'Let your eyelids look straight before you' applies to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said: רבי מאיר is different. The verse 'And let your eyelids look straight before you' was fulfilled in him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו answers the challenge. He says רבי מאיר was a special case, so his story does not undo the general rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule exists because people's memory makes mistakes. רבי מאיר's knowledge of the text was so exact that the danger did not apply to him. The rule stays in place for everyone else.

keyTerms.meaning: Is different: the case is an exception
That is fulfilled in him: the verse describes him
'Let your eyelids look straight before you' (משלי ד:כה)

phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu said:
Rabbi Meir is different,
as in him is fulfilled
'And let your eyelids look straight before you.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ: שָׁאנֵי רַבִּי מֵאִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from step 27.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Personal exception: the story involves a unique individual
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי מאיר's action shows that anyone may write from memory.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי מאיר had perfect command of the text, so his case is an exception and the rule stands for others.

steps.title: What does 'your eyelids look straight' mean?
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא asks רבי ירמיה מדפתי to explain the verse רבי אבהו quoted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא said to רבי ירמיה מדפתי: What does 'And let your eyelids look straight before you' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: Someone asks what the verse means and how it connects to רבי מאיר. This sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Read simply, the verse is about looking straight ahead. It is not clear how it describes perfect memory of the Torah. The question asks for that connection.

keyTerms.meaning: What is: asking for an explanation

phrases.english: Rami bar Ḥama said to
Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti:
What is 'And let your eyelids look straight before you'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of the verse used in step 28.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How the verse describes רבי מאיר's mastery of the text.

steps.title: Torah words slip away easily, yet they stayed exact for רבי מאיר
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה explains that 'eyelids' (עפעפיך) hints at the Torah's words, which fly away quickly (התעיף). For רבי מאיר, they stayed 'straight', meaning exact.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: This refers to the words of Torah. About them it says, 'Will you glance at it, and it is gone?' Even so, they stayed exact for רבי מאיר.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה explains the verse. It describes how the Torah's words, which usually slip away, stayed perfectly in place in רבי מאיר's mind.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a wordplay. עפעפיך (eyelids) shares a root with התעיף (glance fleetingly), from a verse about things that vanish quickly. יישירו (look straight) hints that for רבי מאיר those fleeting words stayed exact (מיושרין).

keyTerms.meaning: 'Will you glance at it, and it is gone?' (משלי כג:ה): things that vanish quickly
Straight, exact: fixed accurately in memory

steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why רבי מאיר is an exception: the reason for the rule, mistakes in memory, did not apply to him.

phrases.english: He said to him: These are the words of Torah,
about which it is written:
'Will you glance at it with your eyes, and it is gone?'
and even so they were exact
for Rabbi Meir.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 29.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The verse describes Torah words, which normally slip away, staying exact in רבי מאיר's memory.

steps.title: רב חסדא stops רב חננאל from writing Torah scrolls from memory
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא saw רב חננאל writing ספרי תורה from memory. He praised his memory but told him that חכמים forbade writing even one letter from memory.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא found רב חננאל writing scrolls without copying from a text. He said to him: The whole Torah is worthy of being written from your memory. But this is what the Sages said: It is forbidden to write even one letter without copying from a written text.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story showing that רבי יוחנן's rule applies even to someone with excellent memory. This sets up a new challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא admits that רב חננאל knows the whole Torah by heart. Even so, he must not write from memory. So perfect memory alone does not create an exception.

keyTerms.meaning: By your mouth: from your own memory

phrases.english: Rav Ḥisda found Rav Ḥananel
writing scrolls
not from a written text.
He said to him:
The entire Torah is fit
to be written from your mouth,
but this is what the Sages said:
It is forbidden to write a single letter
not from a written text.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a story that applies רבי יוחנן's rule even to a sage with perfect memory. This will create tension with steps 28-30.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even someone who knows the whole Torah by heart may not write from memory.

steps.title: If perfect memory is not enough, how could רבי מאיר write?
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא's words show that רב חננאל had perfect memory, and he was still forbidden. So רבי מאיר's perfect memory should not have permitted him either.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since he said 'The whole Torah is fit to be written from your memory', we learn that the words were exact in his mind. Yet רבי מאיר wrote from memory?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא puts the two stories side by side and asks how they fit together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, רבי מאיר was excused because his memory was perfect. רב חננאל also had perfect memory, yet רב חסדא forbade him. So perfect memory cannot be the full reason רבי מאיר was allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: Since he said: introducing an inference from someone's words

phrases.english: Since he said:
The entire Torah is fit
to be written from your mouth,
we infer that they were exact in his memory;
but Rabbi Meir wrote?

steps.triggerLanguage: מִדְּקָאָמַר: כׇּל הַתּוֹרָה כּוּלָּהּ רְאוּיָה שֶׁתִּיכָּתֵב עַל פִּיךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses step 31 to challenge the answer given in steps 28-30.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אבהו's explanation that רבי מאיר was permitted because of his perfect memory
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב חננאל had equally perfect memory and was forbidden. So memory alone cannot explain why רבי מאיר was allowed.

steps.title: An emergency is different
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר wrote only because there was no מגילה at all. In an emergency, an expert may rely on his memory.
steps.simpleTranslation: A time of urgent need is different.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי מאיר's case was an emergency, while רב חננאל's was not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Perfect memory alone is not enough. Writing from memory is allowed only when someone has perfect memory and there is also no other way to fulfill the מצוה. רבי מאיר had no מגילה for פורים, but רב חננאל could have copied from a text.

keyTerms.meaning: A time of urgent need, an emergency

steps.whatToRemember: Writing a holy text from memory is forbidden, even for an expert. רבי מאיר was allowed only because he was an expert and it was an emergency, with no מגילה available.
steps.confusionAlert: The final answer does not throw out רבי אבהו's point about רבי מאיר's memory. It adds a second condition. He needed both perfect memory and an emergency.

phrases.english: A time of exigent circumstances is different.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 32.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing circumstances: emergency versus ordinary time
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Perfect memory alone permits writing from memory, so רב חסדא and רבי מאיר seem to contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: Writing from memory requires both expertise and an emergency. רבי מאיר had both, while רב חננאל had no emergency.

steps.title: אביי allows תפילין and מזוזות to be written from memory
steps.stepSummary: אביי allowed the scribes of the house of בר חבו to write תפילין and מזוזות without copying from a text.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי permitted the house of בר חבו to write תפילין and מזוזות without copying from a written text.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports a ruling by אביי that seems to go against רבי יוחנן's rule. This sets up the next question: whose view is he following?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן said nothing may be written from memory. אביי allows it for תפילין and מזוזות, even with no emergency. This suggests these items have a different rule from Torah scrolls and מגילות.

keyTerms.meaning: תפילין and מזוזות, whose short passages scribes know well

phrases.english: Abaye permitted the house of bar Ḥavu
to write tefillin and mezuzot
not from a written text.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Introduces a ruling that limits רבי יוחנן's rule for certain items.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תפילין and מזוזות may be written from memory.

steps.title: Whose view is אביי following?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which earlier authority supports אביי's lenient ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to whom?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the source of אביי's ruling. This sets up the answer from a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since רבי יוחנן's rule seems to forbid this, אביי's ruling needs support from a תנא.

keyTerms.meaning: According to whom? Asking which authority a ruling follows

phrases.english: In accordance with whom?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of step 34's ruling.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא supports writing תפילין and מזוזות from memory.

steps.title: A ברייתא in the name of רבי: תפילין and מזוזות may be written from memory
steps.stepSummary: אביי follows a ברייתא. In it, רבי ירמיה says in the name of רבי that תפילין and מזוזות may be written from memory and do not need ruled lines.
steps.simpleTranslation: He follows this תנא, as it was taught: רבי ירמיה says in the name of our teacher: תפילין and מזוזות may be written without copying from a text, and they do not need ruled lines.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that אביי's ruling follows a ברייתא. That ברייתא gives two leniencies for תפילין and מזוזות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא shows that some תנאים treat תפילין and מזוזות more leniently than Torah scrolls. They need not be copied from a text, and the parchment does not need etched lines. So אביי has a solid source.

keyTerms.meaning: Like this תנא: identifying the source behind a ruling
In the name of our teacher, meaning רבי יהודה הנשיא
Scoring: etched guide lines on the parchment

steps.whatToRemember: תפילין and מזוזות are an exception. According to this ברייתא, followed by אביי, they may be written from memory and without שרטוט.

phrases.english: In accordance with this tanna,
as it is taught in a baraita:
Rabbi Yirmeya says in the name of our master:
Tefillin and mezuzot may be written
not from a written text,
and they do not require scoring.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 35.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: אביי follows the ברייתא of רבי ירמיה in the name of רבי, which allows תפילין and מזוזות to be written from memory and without שרטוט.

steps.title: The final ruling on ruled lines and writing from memory
steps.stepSummary: The הלכה is that תפילין do not need ruled lines, מזוזות do need ruled lines, and both may be written without copying from a text.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the הלכה is: תפילין do not need ruled lines, but מזוזות do need ruled lines. Both of them may be written without copying from a written text.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the final practical ruling that ends the discussion of אביי's leniency.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא in the previous step said that both תפילין and מזוזות skip ruled lines. The final הלכה accepts that only for תפילין and requires ruled lines for מזוזות. On the second point, writing from memory, the הלכה fully agrees: both may be written without a text in front of the scribe.

keyTerms.meaning: Scored or ruled lines on the parchment that guide the writing
Both this one and that one
Not copied from a written text; written from memory

steps.whatToRemember: תפילין do not need שרטוט, but מזוזות do. Both may be written from memory.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume the הלכה simply follows רבי's ברייתא in every detail. It follows him on writing from memory, but not on ruled lines for מזוזות.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the practical rule scribes follow when they write תפילין and מזוזות.

phrases.english: And the halakha is:
Tefillin do not require scoring,
mezuzot require scoring.
Both these and those may be written
phrases.notes: Refers to both תפילין and מזוזות.

phrases.english: not from a written text.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the practical law after the ברייתא of רבי ירמיה in the name of רבי, partly agreeing and partly differing.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: תפילין need no שרטוט, מזוזות need שרטוט, and both may be written from memory.

steps.title: Why may they be written from memory?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks the reason that תפילין and מזוזות may be written without a text.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why writing from memory is allowed here. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier we learned that even an expert like רב חננאל may not write a ספר from memory. So the גמרא needs to explain why תפילין and מזוזות are different.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind the ruling just given.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why תפילין and מזוזות are an exception to the rule that one must copy from a text.

steps.title: Because scribes know them well
steps.stepSummary: Scribes know these short texts so well that writing them from memory is safe.
steps.simpleTranslation: They are well known (fluent in everyone's mouth).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that scribes know these texts thoroughly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תפילין and מזוזות are short passages that scribes write over and over, so there is little risk of a mistake. A long ספר is different, which is why even an expert like רב חננאל needed a text for it.

keyTerms.meaning: They are well studied and fluent; known by heart

steps.whatToRemember: The exception exists because scribes know these texts by heart, so there is no real risk of error.

phrases.english: They are well known (fluent).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 38.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Scribes are fluent in these short, often-written texts, so writing them from memory carries no real risk of error.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה about invalid writing materials
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה, which says a מגילה written with סם and similar materials is invalid.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: If it was written with סם, and so on, one does not fulfill the obligation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic by quoting the next line of the משנה. This sets up the explanation of each material in the steps that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lists materials that may not be used to write a מגילה: סם, סקרא, קומוס, and קנקנתום. The גמרא will now explain what each of these words means.

keyTerms.meaning: Etc.; short for וְכוּלֵּיהּ, meaning the rest of the quote continues
A writing material listed in the משנה as invalid for a מגילה
Another invalid material, explained below as red paint
Another invalid material, explained below as tree resin

phrases.english: If it was written with sam, etc.
phrases.notes: Quote from the משנה. The full line says one does not fulfill the obligation with such a מגילה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the topic of writing from memory and returns to the next clause of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A מגילה written with סם, סקרא, קומוס, or קנקנתום is invalid.

steps.title: Defining סם
steps.stepSummary: סם is what is called סמא in Aramaic.
steps.simpleTranslation: סם is סמא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the first word in the משנה's list by giving its everyday Aramaic name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא identifies the משנה's Hebrew term with a material people knew by its Aramaic name, so the reader knows exactly which substance is meant.

keyTerms.meaning: The Aramaic name for סם, a type of dye or ink

phrases.english: Sam is samma.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts defining the materials listed in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: סם is the substance known as סמא.

steps.title: Defining סקרא
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר בר חנה says סקרא is called סקרתא, a red paint.
steps.simpleTranslation: As for סקרא, רבה בר בר חנה said: its name is סקרתא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the second material, quoting רבה בר בר חנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This definition is given in the name of a specific אמורא, רבה בר בר חנה. סקרתא is a red paint, which is not proper black ink and so is not valid for a מגילה.

phrases.english: Sikra,
Rabba bar bar Ḥana said:
Its name is sikreta.

steps.triggerLanguage: סִקְרָא, אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues defining the materials listed in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: סקרא is סקרתא, a red paint.

steps.title: Defining קומוס
steps.stepSummary: קומוס is what is called קומא, a tree resin.
steps.simpleTranslation: קומוס is קומא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the third material in the משנה's list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: קומוס is identified as קומא, a sticky tree resin (gum). Like the other materials, it is not proper ink, so a מגילה written with it is invalid.

phrases.english: Komos is koma.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of definitions for the משנה's materials.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: קומוס is קומא, a tree resin.
